{{short description|Field of study in Psychology}}
'''Automatic item generation''' ('''AIG'''), or '''automated item generation''', is a process linking [[Test construction strategies|test construction]] with [[computer programming]]. It uses a [[Algorithm|computer algorithm]] to automatically create [[test item]]s that are the basic building blocks of a [[Psychological testing|psychological test]]. The method was first described by John R. Bormuth<ref>{{cite book |last=Bormuth |first=J. |year=1969 |title=On a theory of achievement test items |url=https://archive.org/details/ontheoryofachiev0000borm |url-access=registration |location=Chicago, IL |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=9780226066301 }}</ref> in the 1960s but was not developed until recently. AIG uses a two-step process: first, a test specialist creates a template called an item model; then, a computer algorithm is developed to generate test items.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Haladyna |first2=T.M. |year=2012 |title=Automatic item generation, theory and practice |location=New York, NY |publisher=Routledge Chapman & Hall |isbn=9780415897518 }}</ref> So, instead of a test specialist writing each individual item, computer algorithms generate families of items from a smaller set of parent item models.<ref name="Blum, Holling"/><ref>{{cite book |last1=Glas |first1=C.A.W. |last2=van der Linden |first2=W.J. |last3=Geerlings |first3=H. |year=2010 |chapter=Estimation of the parameters in an item-cloning model for adaptive testing |editor1-first=W.J. |editor1-last=van der Linden |editor2-first=C.A.W. |editor2-last=Glas |title=Elements of adaptive testing |pages=289–314 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-85461-8_15 |isbn=978-0-387-85459-5 |url=http://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60488/1/126.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240915073355/http://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/60488/1/126.pdf |archive-date=15 September 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Lai |first2=H. |year=2012 |title=The role of item models in automatic item generation |journal=International Journal of Testing |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=273–298 |doi=10.1080/15305058.2011.635830 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/239794821 }}</ref> More recently, [[Neural network (machine learning)|neural networks]], including [[Large Language Model]]s, such as the [[GPT (language model)|GPT]] family, have been used successfully for generating items automatically.<ref name="vonDavier">{{cite journal |last=von Davier |first=M. |title=Automated Item Generation with Recurrent Neural Networks |journal=Psychometrika |volume=83 |pages=847–857 |year=2018 |issue=4 |doi=10.1007/s11336-018-9608-y |pmid=29532403 }}</ref><ref name="Yaneva">{{cite book |editor-last=Yaneva |editor-first=V. |editor2-last=von Davier |editor2-first=M. |year=2023 |title=Advancing Natural Language Processing in Educational Assessment |edition=1st |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9781003278658 |isbn=9781003278658 }}</ref>

==Context==

In [[psychological testing]], the responses of the test taker to test items provide objective measurement data for a variety of human characteristics.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Van der Linden |first1=W.J. |last2=Hambleton |first2=R.K. |year=1997 |chapter=Item Response Theory: a brief history, common models, and extensions |editor-first=R.K. |editor-last=Hambleton |editor2-first=W.J. |editor2-last=van der Linden |title=Handbook of modern Item Response Theory |url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofmodern0000lind |url-access=limited |pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofmodern0000lind/page/n19 1]–31 |location=New York |publisher=Springer |isbn=0-387-94661-6 }}</ref> Some characteristics measured by psychological and educational tests include academic abilities, school performance, [[intelligence]], [[motivation]], etc. and these tests are frequently used to make decisions that have significant consequences on individuals or groups of individuals. Achieving measurement quality standards, such as [[test validity]], is one of the most important objectives for psychologists and educators.<ref>{{cite book |last=Embretson |first=S.E. |year=1999 |chapter=Issues in the measurement of cognitive abilities |editor-first=S.E. |editor-last=Embretson |editor2-first=S.L. |editor2-last=Hershberger |title=The new rules of measurement |pages=1–15 |location=Mahwah |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |doi=10.4324/9781410603593 |isbn=9781410603593 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/44833474 }}</ref>  AIG is an approach to test development which can be used to maintain and improve test quality economically in the contemporary environment where computerized testing has increased the need for large numbers of test items.<ref name=":0" />

==Benefits==

AIG reduces the cost of producing [[standardized test]]s,<ref>{{cite book |last=Rudner |first=L. |year=2010 |chapter=Implementing the graduate management admission test computerized adaptive test |editor-first=W.J. |editor-last=van der Linden |editor2-first=C.A.W. |editor2-last=Glas |title=Elements of adaptive testing |pages=151–165 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-85461-8_15 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/226143316 }}</ref> as algorithms can generate many more items in a given amount of time than a human test specialist. It can quickly and easily create parallel test forms, which allow for different test takers to be exposed to different groups of test items with the same level of complexity or difficulty, thus enhancing test security.<ref name="Blum, Holling" /> When combined with [[computerized adaptive testing]], AIG can generate new items or select which already-generated items should be administered next based on the test taker's ability during the administration of the test. AIG is also expected to produce items with a wide range of difficulty, fewer errors in construction, and is expected to permit higher comparability of items due to a more systematic definition of the prototypical item model.<ref name="Blum, Holling" /><ref name=":o)">{{cite book |last=Irvine |first=S. |year=2002 |chapter=The foundations of item generation for mass testing |editor-first=S.H. |editor-last=Irvine |editor2-first=P.C. |editor2-last=Kyllonen |title=Item generation for test development |pages=3–34 |location=Mahwah |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |isbn=9781138973473 |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/289962970 }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference |last1=Lai |first1=H. |last2=Alves |first2=C. |last3=Gierl |first3=M.J. |year=2009 |title=Using automatic item generation to address item demands for CAT |editor-first=D.J. |editor-last=Weiss |conference=Proceedings of the 2009 GMAC Conference on Computerized Adaptive Testing |url=http://iacat.org/sites/default/files/biblio/cat09lai.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240428033540/http://iacat.org/sites/default/files/biblio/cat09lai.pdf |archive-date=28 April 2024 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Radicals, incidentals and isomorphs==

Test development (including AIG) can be enriched if it is based on any cognitive theory. Cognitive processes taken from a given theory are often matched with item features during their construction. The purpose of this is to predetermine a given psychometric parameter, such as item difficulty (from now on: {{Script|Grek|β}}). Let ''radicals''<ref name=":o)" /> be those structural elements that significantly affect item parameters and provide the item with certain cognitive requirements. One or more radicals of the item model can be manipulated in order to produce parent item models with different parameters (e.g., {{Script|Grek|β}}) levels. Each parent can then grow its own family by manipulating other elements that Irvine<ref name=":o)" /> called ''incidentals''. Incidentals are surface features that suffer random variations from item to item within the same family. Items that have the same structure of radicals and only differ in incidentals are usually labeled as ''isomorphs''<ref>{{cite book |last=Bejar |first=I. I. |year=2002 |chapter=Generative testing: from conception to implementation |title=Item Generation for Test Development |editor-first=S. H. |editor-last=Irvine |editor2-first=P. C. |editor2-last=Kyllonen |location=Mahwah, NJ |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |pages=199–217 |isbn=9781138973473 }}</ref> or ''clones''.<ref name="hello">{{cite journal |last=Embretson |first=S.E. |year=1999 |title=Generating items during testing: psychometric issues and models |journal=Psychometrika |volume=64 |issue=4 |pages=407–433 |doi=10.1007/BF02294564 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/24063316 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M. E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |year=2012 |title=Using automatic item generation to meet the increasing item demands of the high-stakes educational and occupational assessment |journal=Learning and Individual Differences |volume=22 |pages=112–117 |doi=10.1016/j.lindif.2011.11.005 }}</ref>

There can be two kinds of item cloning: On the one hand, the item model may consist of an item with one or more open places, and cloning is done by filling each place with an element selected from a list of possibilities. On the other hand, the item model could be an intact item which is cloned by introducing transformations, for example changing the angle of an object of spatial ability tests.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Glas |first1=C. A. W. |last2=van der Linden |first2=W. J. |year=2003 |title=Computerized adaptive testing with item cloning |journal=Applied Psychological Measurement |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=247–261 |doi=10.1177/0146621603027004001 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237780579 }}</ref> The variation of these items' surface characteristics should not significantly influence the testee's responses. This is the reason why it is believed that incidentals produce only slight differences among the item parameters of the isomorphs.<ref name="Blum, Holling">{{cite journal |last1=Blum |first1=Diego |last2=Holling |first2=Heinz |title=Automatic Generation of Figural Analogies With the IMak Package |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |date=6 August 2018 |volume=9 |article-number=1286 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2018.01286 |pmid=30127757 |pmc=6087760 |doi-access=free }} [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]] The material was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License].</ref>

==Current developments==

A number of item generators have been subjected to objective validation testing.

MathGen is a program that generates items to test mathematical achievement. In a 2018 article for the ''[[Journal of Educational Measurement]]'', authors Embretson and Kingston conducted an extensive qualitative review and empirical try-outs to evaluate the qualitative and psychometric properties of generated items, concluding that the items were successful and that items generated from the same item structure had predictable psychometric properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Embretson |first1=S.E. |last2=Kingston |first2=N.M. |year=2018 |title=Automatic item generation: a more efficient process for developing mathematics achievement items? |journal=Journal of Educational Measurement |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=112–131 |doi=10.1111/jedm.12166 }}</ref><ref>{{cite report |last1=Willson |first1=J. |last2=Morrison |first2=K. |last3=Embretson |first3=S.E. |year=2014 |title=Automatic item generator for mathematical achievement items: MathGen3.0 |work=Technical report IES1005A-2014 for the Institute of Educational Sciences Grant R305A100234 |location=Atlanta, GA |publisher=Cognitive Measurement Laboratory, Georgia, Institute of Technology }}</ref>

A test of melodic discrimination developed with the aid of the computational model Rachman-Jun 2015<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=T. |last2=Laney |first2=R. |last3=Willis |first3=A. |last4=Garthwaite |first4=P.H. |year=2016 |title=Developing and evaluating computational models of music style |journal=Artificial Intelligence for Engineering Design, Analysis and Manufacturing |volume=30 |pages=16–43 |doi=10.1017/S0890060414000687 }}</ref> was administered to participants in a 2017 trial. According to the data collected by P.M. Harrison et al., results demonstrate strong [[test validity|validity]] and [[reliability (psychometric)|reliability]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harrison |first1=P.M. |last2=Collins |first2=T. |last3=Müllensiefen |first3=D. |year=2017 |title=Applying modern psychometric techniques to melodic discrimination testing: item response theory, computerized adaptive testing, and automatic item generation |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=7 |issue=3618 |pages=1–18 |doi=10.1038/s41598-017-03586-z  |doi-access=free|pmid=28620165 |pmc=5472621 |bibcode=2017NatSR...7.3618H }}</ref>

Ferreyra and Backhoff-Escudero<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ferreyra |first1=M.F. |last2=Backhoff-Escudero |first2=E. |year=2016 |title=Validez del Generador Automático de Ítems del Examen de Competencias Básicas (Excoba) |journal=Relieve |language=es, en |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=art. 2, 1–16 |doi=10.7203/relieve.22.1.8048 |doi-access=free }}</ref> generated two parallel versions of the Basic Competences Exam (Excoba), a general test of educational skills, using a program they developed called GenerEx. They then studied the internal structure as well as the psychometric equivalence of the created tests. Empirical results of psychometric quality are favorable overall, and the tests and items are consistent as measured by multiple psychometric indices.

Gierl and his colleagues<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Lai |first2=H. |last3=Pugh |first3=D. |last4=Touchie |first4=C. |last5=Boulais |first5=A.P. |last6=De Champlain |first6=A. |year=2016 |title=Evaluating the psychometric characteristics of generated multiple-choice test items |journal=Applied Measurement in Education |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=196–210 |doi=10.1080/08957347.2016.1171768 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lai |first1=H. |last2=Gierl |first2=M.J. |last3=Byrne |first3=B.E. |last4=Spielman |first4=A.I. |last5=Waldschmidt |first5=D.M. |year=2016 |title=Three modeling applications to promote automatic item generation for examinations in dentistry |journal=Journal of Dental Education |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=339–347 |doi=10.1002/j.0022-0337.2016.80.3.tb06090.x |pmid=26933110 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Lai |first2=H. |year=2013 |title=Evaluating the quality of medical multiple-choice items created with automated processes |journal=Medical Education |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=726–733 |doi=10.1111/medu.12202 |pmid=23746162 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Lai |first2=H. |last3=Turner |first3=S.R. |year=2012 |title=Using automatic item generation to create multiple-choice test items |journal=Medical Education |volume=46 |issue=8 |pages=757–765 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2923.2012.04289.x |pmid=22803753 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229158837 }}</ref> used an AIG program called the Item Generator (IGOR<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gierl |first1=M.J. |last2=Zhou |first2=J. |last3=Alves |first3=C. |year=2008 |title=Developing a taxonomy of item mode types to promote assessment engineering |journal=J Technol Learn Assess |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=1–51 |url=https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ838625 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250201155444/https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ838625 |archive-date=1 February 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref>) to create multiple-choice items that test medical knowledge. IGOR-generated items, even when compared to manually-designed items, showed good psychometric properties.

Arendasy, Sommer, and Mayr<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |last3=Mayr |first3=F. |year=2011 |title=Using automatic item generation to simultaneously construct German and English versions of a Word Fluency Test |journal=Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=464–479 |doi=10.1177/0022022110397360 }}</ref> used AIG to create verbal items to test verbal fluency in German and English, administering them to German- and English-speaking participants respectively. The computer-generated items showed acceptable psychometric properties. The sets of items administered to these two groups were based on a common set of interlanguage anchor items, which facilitated cross-lingual comparisons of performance.

Holling, Bertling, and Zeuch<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holling |first1=H. |last2=Bertling |first2=J.P. |last3=Zeuch |first3=N. |year=2009 |title=Automatic item generation of probability word problems |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_studies-in-educational-evaluation-see_june-september-2009_35_2-3/page/71 |url-access=limited |journal=Studies in Educational Evaluation |volume=35 |issue=2–3 |pages=71–76 |doi=10.1016/j.stueduc.2009.10.004 }}</ref> used [[probability theory]] to automatically generate mathematical word problems with expected difficulties. They achieved a Rasch<ref>{{cite book |last=Rasch |first=G. |orig-date=1960 |title=Probabilistic models for some intelligence and attainment tests |location=Chicago |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=1980 |url=https://archive.org/details/probabilisticmod0000rasc }}</ref> model fit and item difficulties could be explained by the linear logistic test model (LLTM<ref>{{cite journal |last=Fischer |first=G.H. |year=1973 |title=The linear logistic test model as an instrument of educational research |journal=Acta Psychologica |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=359–374 |doi=10.1016/0001-6918(73)90003-6 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281345292 }}</ref>), as well as by the Random-Effects LLTM. Holling, Blank, Kuchenbäcker, and Kuhn<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Holling |first1=H. |last2=Blank |first2=H. |last3=Kuchenbäcker |first3=K. |last4=Kuhn |first4=J.T. |year=2008 |title=Rule-based item design of statistical word problems: a review and first implementation |journal=Psychology Science Quarterly |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=363–378 |url=https://www.psychologie-aktuell.com/fileadmin/download/PschologyScience/3-2008/04_Holling.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241212235830/https://www.psychologie-aktuell.com/fileadmin/download/PschologyScience/3-2008/04_Holling.pdf |archive-date=12 December 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref> made a similar study with statistical word problems but without using AIG. Arendasy and his colleagues<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |last3=Gittler |first3=G. |last4=Hergovich |first4=A. |year=2006 |title=Automatic generation of quantitative reasoning items. A pilot study |journal=Journal of Individual Differences |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=2–14 |doi=10.1027/1614-0001.27.1.2 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228655135 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |year=2007 |title=Using psychometric technology in educational assessment: the case of a schema-based isomorphic approach to the automatic generation of quantitative reasoning items |journal=Learning and Individual Differences |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=366–383 |doi=10.1016/j.lindif.2007.03.005 }}</ref> presented studies on automatically generated algebra word problems and examined how a quality control framework of AIG can affect the measurement quality of items.

=== Automatic generation of figural items ===
[[File:IMak stem example.png|thumb|Four-rule-based figural analogy item automatically generated with the IMak package (for more information, see {{harvnb|Blum|Holling|2018}}).]]

The Item Maker (IMak) is a program written in the [[R (programming language)|R programming language]] for plotting figural analogy items. The psychometric properties of 23 IMak-generated items were found to be satisfactory, and item difficulty based on rule generation could be predicted by means of the linear logistic test model (LLTM).<ref name="Blum, Holling"/><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Yang |first1=Yuan  |first2=Mathilee |last2=Kunda |date=February 8, 2023 |title=Computational Models of Solving Raven's Progressive Matrices: A Comprehensive Introduction |eprint=2302.04238v1  |class=cs.AI}}</ref> Further research confirmed the high [[internal consistency]] of the generated items.<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Fu |first1=Jingcheng |first2=Xing |last2=Zhang |first3=Songfa |last3=Zhong |date=September 29, 2023 |title=Hedging-Based Scoring Rules for Multiple-Choice Questions |ssrn=4009983}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Myszkowski |first1=N. |last2=Storme |first2=M.|last3=Kubiak |first3=E. |last4=Baron |first4=S.|year=2022 |title=Exploring the associations between personality and response speed trajectories in low-stakes intelligence tests |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=191 |issue=111580 |pages=1–9 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2022.111580}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=von Gugelberg |first1=H.M. |last2=Schweizer |first2=K.|last3=Troche|first3=S.J.|year=2025 |title=Experimental evidence for rule learning as the underlying source of the item-position effect in reasoning ability measures |journal=Learning and Individual Differences |volume=118 |issue=102622 |pages=1–11 |article-number=102622 |doi=10.1016/j.lindif.2024.102622|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Büchli |first1=A. |last2=Beckmann |first2=J.F.|last3=Troche|first3=S.J.|year=2026 |title=Differential effects of social and digital feedback interventions in the Figural Analogies Learning Test (FALT) |journal=Journal of Intelligence |volume=14 |issue=134 |pages=1–20 |article-number=14070134|doi=10.3390/jintelligence14070134 |doi-access=free |pmid=42505945 |pmc=13412734 }}</ref>

MazeGen is another program coded with R that generates mazes automatically. The psychometric properties of 18 such mazes were found to be optimal, including [[Rasch model]] fit and the LLTM prediction of maze difficulty.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loe |first1=B.S. |last2=Rust |first2=J. |year=2017 |title=The perceptual maze test revisited: evaluating the difficulty of automatically generated mazes |journal=Assessment |volume=26 |issue=8 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.1177/1073191117746501 |pmid=29239208 }}</ref>

GeomGen is a program that generates figural matrices.<ref name="geom">{{cite book |last=Arendasy |first=M. |year=2002 |title=Geom-Gen-Ein Itemgenerator für Matrizentestaufgaben |language=de |location=Viena |publisher=Eigenverlag }}</ref> A study which identified sources of measurement bias related to response elimination strategies for figural matrix items concluded that distractor salience favors the pursuit of response elimination strategies and that this knowledge could be incorporated into AIG to improve the [[construct validity]] of such items.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |year=2013 |title=Reducing response elimination strategies enhances the construct validity of figural matrices |journal=Intelligence |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=234–243 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2013.03.006 }}</ref> The same group used AIG to study [[differential item functioning]] (DIF) and gender differences associated with [[mental rotation]]. They manipulated item design features that have exhibited gender DIF in previous studies, and they showed that the estimates of the [[effect size]] of gender differences were compromised by the presence of different kinds of gender DIF that could be related to specific item design features.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |year=2010 |title=Evaluating the contribution of different item features to the effect size of the gender difference in three-dimensional mental rotation using automatic item generation |journal=Intelligence |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=574–581 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2010.06.004 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |last3=Gittler |first3=G. |year=2010 |title=Combining automatic item generation and experimental designs to investigate the contribution of cognitive components to the gender difference in mental rotation |journal=Intelligence |volume=38 |issue=5 |pages=506–512 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2010.06.006 }}</ref>

Arendasy also studied possible violations of the psychometric quality identified using [[item response theory]] (IRT) of automatically generated visuospatial reasoning items. For this purpose, he presented two programs, namely: the already-mentioned GeomGen<ref name="geom" /> and the Endless Loop Generator (EsGen). He concluded that GeomGen was more suitable for AIG because IRT principles can be incorporated during item generation.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Arendasy |first=M. |year=2005 |title=Automatic generation of Rasch-calibrated items: figural matrices test GEOM and Endless-Loops Test EC |journal=International Journal of Testing |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=197–224 |doi=10.1207/s15327574ijt0503_2 }}</ref> In a parallel research project using GeomGen, Arendasy and Sommer<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arendasy |first1=M.E. |last2=Sommer |first2=M. |year=2005 |title=The effect of different types of perceptual manipulations on the dimensionality of automatic generated figural matrices |journal=Intelligence |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=307–324 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2005.02.002 }}</ref> found that variation of the perceptual organization of items could influence the performance of respondents depending on their ability levels and that it had an effect on several psychometric quality indices. With these results, they questioned the unidimensionality assumption of figural matrix items in general.

MatrixDeveloper<ref>{{cite book |last=Hofer |first=S. |year=2004 |title=MatrixDeveloper |location=Münster, Germany |publisher=Psychological Institute IV. Westfälische Wilhelms-Universität }}</ref> was used to generate twenty-five 4x4 [[square matrix]] items automatically. These items were administered to 169 individuals. According to research results, the items show a good [[Rasch model]] fit, and rule-based generation can explain the item difficulty.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Freund |first1=P.A. |last2=Hofer |first2=S. |last3=Holling |first3=H. |year=2008 |title=Explaining and controlling for the psychometric properties of computer-generated figural matrix items |journal=Applied Psychological Measurement |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=195–210 |doi=10.1177/0146621607306972 }}</ref>

The first known item matrix generator was designed by Embretson,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Embretson |first=S.E. |year=1998 |title=A cognitive design system approach to generating valid tests: application to abstract reasoning |journal=Psychological Methods |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=380–396 |doi=10.1037/1082-989X.3.3.380 }}</ref><ref name="hello" /> and her automatically generated items demonstrated good psychometric properties, as it is shown by Embretson and Reise.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embretson |first1=S.E. |last2=Reise |first2=S.P. |year=2000 |title=Item Response Theory for psychologists |url=https://archive.org/details/itemresponsetheo0000embr |url-access=limited |location=Mahwah |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |doi=10.4324/9781410605269 |isbn=978-0805828191 }}</ref> She also proposed a model for adequate online item generation.
